title: Interaction-Induced Bloch Geometry and Transverse Thermoelectric Transport
authors: Heng-Yu Di, YuanDong Wang, Zhen-Gang Zhu, Gang Su
abstract: Electron--electron interactions can reconstruct Bloch wave functions, changing their geometry and the associated thermoelectric response. We derive the linear thermoelectric response within the Hartree--Fock (HF) approximation using the thermal length-gauge density-matrix approach, resolving Drude, symmetric quantum-metric, and antisymmetric Berry-curvature contributions. In a noninteracting Bloch eigenbasis, we separate the reconstructed Berry connection into the noninteracting connection and an interaction connection. This gives bare, coherence, and interaction-connection contributions to the anomalous thermoelectric response. We determine the constraints imposed by spatial inversion, rotational, time-reversal, and combined symmetries on the three transport channels. In the relaxation-time approximation, the leading weak-broadening behavior is $Γ^{-1}$ for the Drude contribution, $Γ$ for the quantum-metric contribution, and $Γ^0$ for the Berry-curvature contribution. The interband scalings apply away from band degeneracies. Self-consistent calculations for the triangular-lattice extended Hubbard model illustrate how interactions generate Berry curvature and a quantum metric, change the symmetry of the system, and thereby contribute to transverse thermoelectric transport.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes how electron-electron interactions modify the electronic band structure geometry, leading to changes in thermoelectric transport. Using the Hartree-Fock approximation and a density-matrix formalism, the authors decompose the anomalous response into contributions from the Drude, quantum-metric, and Berry-curvature terms. The results demonstrate that interactions generate measurable geometric properties that dictate the material's thermoelectric response.
main_problem: The paper investigates how electron-electron interactions reconstruct Bloch wave functions, thereby altering the geometry of the electronic bands and the resulting transverse thermoelectric response.
main_result: Interactions generate Berry curvature and a quantum metric, which contribute distinct, quantifiable terms to the anomalous thermoelectric transport, which can be analyzed via symmetry constraints.
method: The linear thermoelectric response is derived using the thermal length-gauge density-matrix approach within the Hartree-Fock (HF) approximation.
model_or_system: The analysis uses a tight-binding model extended to include electron-electron interactions, specifically illustrated with self-consistent calculations on the triangular-lattice extended Hubbard model.
key_observables:
Thermoelectric response tensor ($\alpha_{\mu
u}$), Drude contribution, quantum-metric contribution, and Berry-curvature contribution.
important_parameters: Broadening parameter ($\Gamma$), interaction strength ($V$), and symmetry constraints (spatial inversion, time-reversal).
main_assumptions: The analysis employs the relaxation-time approximation (RTA) for broadening and relies on mean-field eigenstates derived from the HF approximation.
figures_summary: The notes mention symmetry constraints (Table I & II) and specific results from the triangular-lattice model (Appendix F), but no explicit figure descriptions are provided.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by deriving the linear response using the density matrix approach, decomposing the response into intra- and interband parts, separating the interband response into symmetric and antisymmetric channels, and finally analyzing the contributions of the bare, coherence, and interaction-induced terms.
why_interesting: While focused on transport, the explicit treatment of interaction-induced geometric terms (Berry curvature, quantum metric) and the use of mean-field theory for correlated systems connects to understanding emergent quantum geometric effects in strongly interacting quantum materials.
